newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia July retail trade data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia July retail trade data.

text.p: Australian retail trade rose 2.4 percent in July, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said.
Economists had been expecting a rise of 0.4 percent, with forecasts only ranging as high as 1.0 percent.
A selection of economists immediate reactions follows.
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"Well there's no doubt that this number was a surprise, it was above the top end of market expectations and does suggest that some of the earlier weakness we had seen in retail spending was somewhat misstated. It's probably more consistent with what we think is happening to the household sector -- employment, while weak at the moment, has risen for four months running, wages are running at four to five percent, and really the only doubt on the consumer spending side had been some fall in consumer sentiment ahead of the budget. Now that the budget has been pretty much accepted by the wider community, we would expect it consumer sentiment to recover."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"Retail trade data does look very volatile at the moment. It's probably enough to hold the line on any monetary policy changes, but it may still be there depending on what the data shows looking out towards November. The issue is, is this the beginning of some rebound in activity running into late 1996/97, or is it just a temporary blip?"
NIGEL DOUGLAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH AUSTRALIA:

"These July numbers tend to produce surprises on the upside, as consumers shift their spending patterns to coincide with July sales from the retailing sector. In the retail sector there's been a lot of downward pressure on prices and that would have boosted volumes considerably. I think we'll see the (bond and bill) selloff go a little bit further because the market had rallied along way, and probably had got excessively gloomy about growth prospects in the short term."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, SENIOR ECONOMIST AT CITIBANK AUSTRALIA

"At face value you would have to say it looks reasonably bearish (for the bond market). The consumer is back in town and spending a bit of money. Clearly the discounting policies of the retailers is having an impact on consumer demand."
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"Clearly higher than expected. There's a comment there that clearance sales by department stores has probably spilled between the months, so it's upset the seasonal adjustment. So taking the two months together, maybe retail sales haven't been as weak as we were expecting, but maybe perversely the strength is a sign of the weakness because the department stores have had to (discount) to really clear their stocks. Also, if it is clearance store sales, and if there has been price cutting to move stock, then that's also good for the inflation numbers.
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH:

"The retail trade numbers are fairly volatile month to month. It's all department stores ... so it all has probably got to do with seasonal analysis. I would tend to discount this number quite a bit. Thinking about the current state of strength of demand in the economy, I wouldn't be placing a too much weight on it. Certainly it is a strong number and underlying that is probably some reasonably strong spending figures but ... you should treat it with caution."
